en: Having bowed to those Arhats by whose illustrious names success in all desired fortunes is attained, I compose this commentary on the *Kaṅkāla-adhyāya*.
Having heard something from my gurus, having synthesized some [from their teachings] with those who know that [reality],
and having experienced something myself, this treatise is being commented upon by me.
Even when taught directly by the Guru, the alchemical process (dhātuvāda) is not accomplished as long as the ritual procedure has not been witnessed two or three times in the presence of the Guru.
Therefore, having heard this or even having seen it anywhere else,
the foolish, by expending their wealth, suffer in vain.
If the true guru, having become gracious, should demonstrate the entire ritual action even in play,
then all yogas will undoubtedly be accomplished.

Therefore, even when the meaning of the text has been clearly explained here, one should not exert effort in the practice of alchemy (*dhātuvāda*), disregarding the Guru, because of the lack of primary certainty [regarding its efficacy].
He who speaks does not know; he who knows does not speak.
Therefore, wise men should not extend their mouths [in speech] anywhere at all.
The venerable Kaṅkālaya, who was proficient in mercury, pills, and ointments, explained the true nature of mercury for the sake of training his own disciples. (Rasādhyāya 8)
The virtuous disciple of Śrīkaṅkālaya, for the benefit of himself and others,
has composed this chapter on aesthetic flavor (*rasādhyāya*), consisting of twenty-one sections.
[1] Therein, at the very beginning, he states the salutation to his chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*) for the sake of accomplishing the task undertaken without obstacles.
Having first prostrated before the illustrious Bhairava, the omniscient Lord of the three worlds,
I salute the illustrious Bhāratī and Vighneśa for the pacification of obstacles.
Celibacy, austerity, and the consumption of sacrificial food (haviṣya) must be practiced;

for those fallen from ritual action, these do not succeed, and for those whose austerity has perished, they bear no fruit. (Rsdhy 11) [In this regard, there are eighty-four types of alchemical operations (rasakarma), eighty-four varieties of pills (guṭikā), and eighty-four kinds of collyriums (añjana). (1)
* Thus, there are two hundred and fifty-two such divisions. 2.

* Then, from among these divisions, when any particular rite is commenced, at that time a month of austerity in the form of celibacy (*brahmacarya*) must be performed prior to the commencement. 3. * This is because celibacy alone is the root of all austerity. 4.
5. Because everything devoid of that [austerity] and lacking fervor is fruitless.
6. Or rather, celibacy (brahmacarya) should be maintained.
7. Furthermore, austerity should be practiced by means of a teacher and so forth, according to the proper method.
Because both [the donor and the recipient] share the same primordial root for all karmic fruits.
(8) Likewise, one should prepare sacrificial food (*haviṣyānna*) mixed with ghee and sugar, such as milk-rice (*pāyasa*) or a meal of milk.
(9) This is because there is no purification of the body through other types of food. (10)

"And because of the absence of the means for breath-control (prāṇāyāma) [it does not succeed]. (11) Therefore, by one who thus maintains the ritual action, the fruit of that action must be brought to completion. (12) For the operations such as the extraction of the essences (rasa) do not succeed when the practitioner has failed, that is, when he does not perform the prescribed eating. (13)
"When austerity is lost, they do not bear fruit.
(14) And he himself will clarify this at the end of the book.
(15) Now, the chapter of the illustrious Kaṅkālaya-yogin has arrived.
"I speak of that chapter where the essence of the chain (*śṛṅkhalārasa*) is manifested through logical methods.
[Note: This is the disciple’s statement, "I speak," regarding the chapter received from the presence of the illustrious Kaṅkālaya-yogin.
(1) In that chapter, the essence of the chain is made manifest by means of logical methods—namely, the procedures for medicinal processing, infusion, and heating in a crucible (*puṭapāka*). (2)]
Just as a chain is connected through the mutual interpenetration of its preceding and succeeding links, so it is here as well.
First is the purification of the mercury;
then, the revivification of the purified mercury that has been solidified.
6. The casting down of one who has been raised up from a swoon;
7. The raising up again of one who has been cast down;
8. The fomentation of one who has been cast down and raised up.
9. And for that which has been fomented by sweating, there is the state of being restrained.
10. For that which has been restrained, there is the state of being suppressed. 11. And for that which has been suppressed, there is the extension of the crooked [limb].
12. And the digestion of mica by means of *vakraprasārita* [mercury].
13. And the digestion of iron by means of mica that has been digested.
14. And the digestion of iron that has been digested by means of the streaks shining like steel.
15. And by means of the king of light that has been digested (jīrṇa), there is the digestion of the king of gold (hemarāji).
16. By means of the king of gold that has been digested, there is the digestion of sulphur (gandhaka).
17. And by means of the sulphur that has been digested, there is the digestion of the essence of realgar (manaḥśilāsattva).
And the digestion of the essence of copper by means of the digested essence of mica;
(18) and the digestion of the essence of iron and diamonds by means of the digested essence of copper; (19) and the binding of the digested diamond. (20)

23. And the transference of that which has been killed.

Thus, the reality is that the subsequent refinement (*saṃskāra*) of a mercury (*rasa*) is bound to its preceding and even more preceding refinements; this is what is being stated. [27] Next, I shall describe the defects of mercury, its purification prior to refinement, the results of the mercurial essences, their production, and the alchemy of the body and metals. [Rsdhy_13]
*1. Regarding the twelve defects of mercury (*sūta*) and lead (*pārada*);

*2. through the means for removing those defects, I shall first describe their purification and stainlessness, as well as the eighteen processing techniques (*saṃskāra*), beginning with *pāṭa* and *sāraṇā*; *3.
thereafter, the fruit consisting of the production of silver (*tāra*) and other metals from the processed juices (*rasa*).
"Then [I shall explain] the production of gold, kingdoms, and so forth, as well as copper, beings, and so forth;
then the alchemy for achieving the body and the alchemy for achieving iron—this is the statement of the disciple of Śrīkaṅkālaya. (vv. 4–5)
In this regard, he states the answer to the proposition in due order:
[6] "The first pair consists of one made of clay and a sheath; the second pair is a stone sheath;
the third is born of water; and two each are produced from lead and tin."
In Vaṅga there is Kapālin and Kālikā; in Nāga, Śyāma and Kapālinī;
and whatever form Tarā has when she is in milk, those two Kapālikās are of that same form.
The five colors are as follows: Śyāmā, Kālikā, and Kṛṣṇavarṇikā; these seven innate coverings (kañcukas) are always produced from mercury. (Rsdhy_16) [These three verses are also clear. 1.

The two defects arising from tin (*vaṅga*) and the "dark-colored fragment" (*śyāmakapālikā*)—these sixth and seventh [defects] arise from lead (*nāga*). He states the characteristics of these four: 5.
When milk has been boiled, whatever kind of scum (*tarā*) appears on the surface; 6. A similar [scum] appears in the juice as well—that is the defect arising from tin. 7.
And the *kapālikā* [flaw] is one that has a *nāga* above it. (8) *Śyāmā* is the sixth flaw; it is five-colored. *Kālikā* is the fifth flaw; it is black in color.
(9) Now, he states the five flaws of the mercury (*rasa*). (10)
The first fault is that of impurity; the second arises from fire;
the third is the fault of poison; and the fourth is known as pride.
The fifth defect is "madness" (*unmatta*); these are the five defects always present in a *rasa*. [This half-verse is clear.
And here, those things which are seen within water due to contact with earth, stone, or another liquid, as well as those on the surface of milk like froth, are called *kañcukas* (shrouds).
Furthermore, the specific distinction is that those which become intoxicated by *kodrava* grains are the defects (*doṣas*).
Now, he describes the individual transformations of these defects:
"From an earthen casing, leprosy (*kuṣṭha*) arises in embodied beings. (Rsdhy 18)
From stone arises dullness (*jāḍya*), and from water arises a mass of wind (*vātastoma*);
these two produce *cilharī* in the body, as do tin, lead, and bone. (Rsdhy 19)
The Kālikā [fever] always causes elephantiasis,
ringworm, jaundice, delusion, indigestion, and jaundice.
White leprosy arises from the husk of *śyāmāka* grain;
the impurity produced by mercury destroys the vital energy of the body.
Fire causes the destruction of living beings, and poison produces a toxic fume; through pride, a limb indeed bursts asunder,
and from intoxication, madness arises.
If one should give mercury that is possessed of the twelve defects,
the sins of killing a Brahmin and other such killings shall always accrue to him.
He who bestows the Lord of Mercury (pārada), freed from the twelve defects,
shall become exalted in this world and a partaker of heaven in the next.

Freed from the twelve defects, the mercury (rasa) renders the body free from disease; when processed by the eightfold refinements, it transforms the body into iron. [All eight verses are indeed clear; however, *cilharī* is simply a specific type of leprosy.]

Thus ends the description of the defects and qualities of the mercury (*sūta*). In the preparation of mercury, there are eighteen purificatory processes (*saṃskāras*): among them, the first is *pāṭasāraṇa*, the second is named *mardana*, and the third is considered to be *śodhana*.
The fourth is the arousal of the *mūrchana*, the fifth is the precipitation of the *rasa*,
the sixth is the elevation of the *rasa*, and the seventh is the sweating (*svedana*).
The eighth is declared the director (niyāmaka), the ninth the restrainer (nirodhaka),
the tenth the opener (mukhakārī), and the one numbered as Rudra (eleventh) is indeed the digester (jāraṇa).
The one marked by the sun is declared to be Bandha; Sāraṇa resides in the Yakṣas;
Māraṇa shall have the number of Manu (14) as its mark; and Pratisāraṇa has the lunar days (15) as its mark.
The sixteenth stage is *krāmaṇa*, the seventeenth is *vedha*, and the eighteenth is *saṃskāra*; by those who know it, this is considered *udghāṭana*. (Rsdhy_30) [The five verses are clear. 1.
* These are the eighteen purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) of mercury (*sūta*).
Now, explaining the purificatory rites in their proper sequence, he says: [3] When the mercury has been strained through a cloth, the purificatory rite is called *pāṭasāraṇa*.
All transformations, such as tin, lead, and so forth, remain upon the cloth.
[First, the mercury is to be strained through a fine cloth so that all previously mentioned impurities, such as tin and lead, adhere to the cloth and remain there.
This is the first purification: the removal by straining (*pāṭasāraṇa*).]
To remove the blackness [of mercury], one should employ *loṣṭajīkaka* derived from lead;
one *pala* of that and sixty-four *palas* of lead.
Having placed it in a mortar and mixed it well, one should grind it for the duration of one *yāma*.
Once ground, it becomes stainless and certainly abandons its blackness.
(Rsdhy_33) [One *pala* of well-prepared white *loṣṭajīkaka* and sixty-four *palas* of mercury—having mixed both and placed them in a mortar, one should grind them for one *prahara*.]
Just as mercury becomes stainless after discarding its blackness, so is the second refinement, *mardana* (rubbing).
[2] When rubbed with the milk of the *vajrī* plant for seven days, the earth-born impurity departs;
when rubbed with the milk of the sun-plant (*arka*) for seven days, the stone-like coating departs. Rsdhy_34.
1. Having placed the mercury in a mortar with the milk of *snuhī*, it is rubbed for seven days.
2. Thereupon, the earth-born coating departs.
3. Rubbed in this manner for seven days with the milk of *arka*, the stone coating departs.
One should roll the leaf-cups (*parpaṭa*) of the *brahmavṛkṣa* tree, moistened with water, into a paste;
by grinding them with their own juice for seven days, the "water-skin" (*ambukañcuka*) departs.
[Note: Having soaked the leaf-cups of the *palāśa* tree in water, one should then roll them, squeeze them through a cloth, and extract the juice.]
By that liquid, the mercury is rubbed for seven days;
[in this way] it becomes like a water-born shell.
From [mercury] ground with the decoction of *citraka*, the *kāpālī* state arises from tin.
From the powder of *vajrakandara* itself, *kālikā* is produced from tin.
The *śyāmā* born of a *nāga* perishes from [an ointment] ground with the juice of *kaṭutumbī*;
the *kapālī* born of a *nāga* perishes from [an ointment] well-ground with the juice of *bīyā*.
The impurities (*kañcukas*) of mercury are destroyed by means of flour for seven times seven days. [The two and a half verses are clear. 1.
Pure *vajra* and the root of *snuhī*, as well as *śūraṇa*—by the juice of these two... 2.
Alternatively, the bulb known as *vajra* grows on mountainous ground.

(3) All the impurities (*kañcuka*) are destroyed by grinding the mercury for seven days with the aforementioned juice. (4) Thus, the impurity is indeed eliminated when [the mercury] is ground with a decoction of the three myrobalans (*triphalā*). (Rsdhy 38)
The defect of fire is destroyed by [the powder] ground with a decoction of *citraka*;
likewise, the defect of poison is pacified by the juice of *aśvagandhā*.
For the fault of pride is not destroyed by being ground with the juice of external objects;
likewise, even a madman dissolves when ground with the juice of the *kudhya* plant.
Indeed, by seven times seven days [forty-nine days] of grinding, the five defects are destroyed;
thus, freed from the twelve defects, the mercury becomes pure.
[The three and a half verses are clear.
1 Only the *aśvagandhā* is the joint.
2] At the end of each medicinal herb, one should wash it with fermented rice-gruel (*kāñjika*).

The purification of the mercury (sūta) should be performed with eleven medicinal herbs. Regarding this, the traditional instruction (*āmnāya*) is as follows: 1. The juice of the aforementioned medicinal herbs is poured over the mercury in a mortar (*khalva*). 2. [The mercury is then rubbed.]
3. As the mercury sinks, it should be ground accordingly.
4. If the preceding medicinal juice dries up gradually, then it should be added again. 5.
If the mercury has been thus ground for seven days, then the mortar is filled with sour gruel (kāñjika) once more.
Then, it is gradually rubbed; thereafter, cotton wicks are inserted, and as they are released, the ends of the wicks touch the ground.
By means of these, the *kāñjika* (sour gruel) flows out.
In this manner, the mercury (*sūta*) is ground with all the medicinal herbs for seven days, and afterwards, it must be washed with *kāñjika*.
And these eleven medicinal herbs: 8.
Vajrakṣīra; 9. Arkakṣīra; 10. [and so forth].

*Aṅkudhya* // 20. Here, the decoction of *citraka* is used twice; therefore, although there are twelve medicinal substances, there are only eleven [distinct items]. This is the third purification process for the processing of mercury (*sūta*). // 21.
The natural mercury, having been crushed with a decoction of the three pungents (*trikaṭu*), is purified.
And likewise with the juice of asanadudhī, and with the juice of ārdra.
In this manner, with the juice of *kākamācī* and the juice of *devadālī*,
one should repeatedly grind it when dry and then dry it again after each time it has been rubbed.
At the conclusion of each medicinal substance, one should wash it with fermented rice-gruel (kāñjika);
for every medicine, one should grind it here for exactly seven days.
The rousing of the fainted [mercury] is produced by five medicinal substances;
mercury that has been raised from its fainting state necessarily becomes radiant.
[Note: Mercury purified according to the previous method should first be ground for seven days with the decoction of the three pungents (trikaṭu) as before in a mortar, and then dried.]
* Then it should be washed with sour gruel (kāñjika).

Afterwards, with the juice of *devadālī* (5), having rubbed [the mercury] for seven days at a time and dried it, it should be washed with fermented rice-gruel (*kāñjika*). When this has been done, that mercury is said to have risen from its swoon and becomes radiant. (7)
Thus ends the fourth [section], the refinement for reviving the swooned [mercury].
When the mercury, resembling collyrium, having abandoned its dense flickeringness, becomes thoroughly coagulated, then it should be known as being of various colors in some instances. Rsdhy_47.
One should raise it up and then cause it to cease within the cavity of the vessel;
then one should cause that mercury to faint again, whereby the *kañcukīs* are destroyed.

In this manner, one should cause the mercury to swoon in this sequence for seven times; thus, the mercury, having been thoroughly swooned, becomes free from defects. [Now follows another view on the revival.]
The wise alchemist should raise the swooned mercury using *āranāla* as a substitute for wine;
and of the mercury that has been raised from its swoon, sixty-four *palas* [should be taken].
Having placed sixteen *palas* of copper powder into a mortar,
one should add the juice of a cut lemon in a thirty-two-fold proportion.

One should grind them until a paste (*pīṭhī*) is formed that resembles ointment. [The meaning is as follows: sixty-four *palas* of mercury that has been revived after being solidified, sixteen *palas* of the finest copper powder, and nine *palas* of salt for the thirty-second part.
Having combined all these together and ground them with the juice of *nimbuka* fruit, one should prepare a paste resembling ointment.
This is the traditional instruction here:

(3) whatever the quantity of the liquid may be, one-fourth part copper powder [should be added], and in the thirty-second part, salt. (4) And lime juice should be poured into it so that the entire medicinal substance sinks. (5)

There is no fault if [the amount] is excessive, but there is a fault if it is deficient. (6) It should be added again whenever it becomes dry. (7) And it should be rubbed until the paste has the consistency of a cosmetic ointment. (8)
Having released it from the mouth of the cauldron, one should place it inside a cloth pouch;
one should smear the edges of the cloth with clay as if they were already fused together within the vessel.
One should place the large pot quickly into the mouth of a water-filled vessel;
likewise, one should smear cloth and clay upon the neck and the joint of the pot.
One should burn the charcoal from the crucible for half a watch (yāma) in such a way that the mercury enters the water while the copper remains in the crucible.
This process of purifying the extraction of mercury (*rasapātana*) should be performed seven times;
thus, the subtle defects are dissolved during the falling [of the mercury] after it has been swooned and raised. [Note:
In a cauldron resembling half a jar, a coil of clay is made at the bottom; this is called the "binding of the cauldron."]

Then, having placed that previously prepared pedestal there upon the neck of the cauldron, and having struck a fold of smooth cloth over it for the purpose of covering, one should smear the edges of that cloth all around with smooth clay so that they become as if fused together. 2.

Then, having placed that crucible inverted over the mouth of a pot half-filled with water, and having applied a firm seal of cloth and clay at the junction where the neck of the pot meets the base of the crucible, cow-dung fuel is ignited inside the crucible for a period of four *ghaṭikās*.
Then, by the heat of the fire, the mercury escapes through the pores of the cloth fibers and enters into the water situated within the lower pot.
Furthermore, the copper remains adhered only to the budha [crucible].

(5) Then, once again, having prepared a crucible of copper powder and mercury as before, the mercury is precipitated into water using a vessel containing water placed over the neck of a cauldron (*kaṭāha*), as previously described.
(6) When this precipitation of the mercury has been performed seven times in this manner, subtle defects such as dullness and sluggishness depart. (7)
Thus ends the fifth [chapter]: the processing of precipitation (*pātana*) for the mercury that has been revived from its swoon.
One should grind the mercury together with *khaḷva* for three days;
one should precipitate it as before, both downwards, upwards, and transversely.
In this manner, one should cause the mercury and the mica— both together— to fall seven times by means of the *pātana* apparatus, rubbing them thoroughly with *kāñjika* juice.
That prepared pill (golaka) should also be placed in the middle of the bottom of a vessel [filled with oil],
along with equal parts of triphalā, rājikā, fire [i.e., cinnabar], poison, and śigru.
Having thoroughly smeared the upper vessel, one should fashion an excellent casket;
having encased the seam with clay, this is the supreme *ḍamaru* yantra.
Furthermore, a supreme Kuṇḍalinī should be established in its upper portion;
below that, one should kindle the fire very gently for three watches of the night.
Having discarded the lower vessel, one should proceed with the upper vessel;
for a period of days, equal parts of ferrous sulfate (kāsīsa), rock salt (saindhava), and mercury (sūta) should be used;
indeed, in the absence of ferrous sulfate, *phullatūrikā* should be given.
One should add [the ingredients] little by little into the mortar and grind the three together;
each [ingredient] should be exactly one hundred *niṣkas*, neither less nor more at any time.
One should cook it for a day with a fierce fire using the *sthālīsampuṭa* apparatus;
once it has become pure and adhered to the upper part, one should extract that auspicious mercury.
Having made light leafs of copper into a paste with three times as much juice in a vessel,
the mercury is separated from the copper and the copper from the mercury for the purpose of precipitation (*pātana*).
Having likewise ground both together, a *pīṭhī* (cake) should be prepared as before.
One should then place that crucible made of copper into another vessel;
having turned the vessel upside down, one should smear its opening with cloth-clay (vastramṛd).
That which is called the *ḍamaruka* yantra, as well as the one named *vidyādhara*,
should have cow dung placed upon the junction of the vessel's rim.
One should cook the mixture with a mild fire in a vessel placed below a *bundha* (sealing lid);
the mercury (*sūta*) moves upward into the upper vessel, while the copper remains right there.
This process of raising the mercury (*sūtotthāpana*) is said to be performed seven times;
the mercury, having been precipitated and then raised, becomes pervasive and clear.

[In the previous formulation, for the purpose of the purification by precipitation (*pātana-saṃskāra*), the copper was separated from the mercury and the mercury from the copper, each being processed separately for seven cycles.]

In this yoga as well, that very same procedure shall be performed; however, the distinction is that while there it was for the purpose of causing a fall, here it is for the purpose of raising up one who has already fallen.
And it is as follows:

having ground sixty-six palas of mercury, sixteen palas of copper filings, and two palas of salt together with the juice of *nimbuka* fruits, one should prepare a paste (*pīṭhī*) as previously described.

Having prepared [the mixture] and placed it in a pot, one should place another pot over it with its opening facing down; at the junction of the two openings, it is smeared with a paste of cloth and clay.
This is called the "Ḍamaruka" and also the "Vidyādhara" yantra.
Then, having applied cow dung to the exterior side of the rim of the upper pot, a gentle fire should be ignited for about one watch (yāma) beneath the rim of the lower pot.
7. Then the mercury (sūta), having flown up, goes into the upper vessel.
8. And the copper remains in the lower vessel.
9. In this manner, when the raising of the mercury is performed seven times repeatedly, the mercury becomes pervasive (vyāpaka).
"Penetrating" (*vyāpaka*) means that which is sharp and of a diffusive nature.
Thus ends the sixth [process], the refinement for raising up the fallen essence. One should prepare the leaves of the *śigru* tree with water as follows:
The mass becomes exceedingly soft; one should then form the *kulhaḍī* (mold) of the mass.
Having discarded the copper, one should throw that entire mercury (sūta), which has risen up and been crushed into thirty-two parts,
into the middle of the previously prepared *kulhaḍī*.
One should pour fermented rice-gruel (āranāla) and juice extracted from nimbuka fruit into the vessel;
one should tie a piece of wood around its neck and attach a previously prepared cloth filter (kulhaḍī).
One should tie the cloth to a piece of wood so that it does not touch the sour gruel;
likewise, one should kindle a gentle fire beneath the covered pot.
Indeed, for seven days, this should be performed every day for eight watches;
and every day, a fresh *kulhaḍikā* should be prepared with *śigru* leaves.
Whenever the *cāranāla* is lost, one should repeatedly add fresh [substance];
the procedure for the sweating (*svedana*) of the mercury should be performed using a *dolāyantra*.
Through sudation, the fire has been kindled and the rasa has become hungry;
now, with its rasa directed upwards, it excessively endures the fire during digestion.
[Having rolled the leaves of the tree named *śigru*, which are as smooth as oil, into a ball, one should prepare a *kulhaḍī* with them.]

Having placed [the ingredients] in that crucible according to the previously mentioned procedure, having discarded the copper, and having added mercury along with salt in the thirty-second part, one should bind that crucible in a cloth; having tied that cloth to a wooden stick with a cord, and having tied a small strip of cloth around the neck of the vessel, one should place inside the vessel sour gruel (kāñjika) mixed with one-third part of lime juice (nimbu-rasa).

Having placed [the substance] over the sour gruel (kāñjika) and tied a cloth in such a way that it is suspended, one should release the *kulhaḍī* so that the sour gruel does not adhere [to it], but only the steam adheres.
Then, for a day and night, a fire should be maintained beneath the vessel.
Then again, having prepared a fresh *kulhaḍī* (vessel) with *śigru* leaves, the mercury should be subjected to sweating for a day and night using the *dolāyantra* in the same manner.
(3) And if the preceding sour gruel (*kāñjika*) dries up, fresh sour gruel should be added.
(4) Thus, after being sweated seven times over seven days with seven *kulhaḍīs*, the mercury, when subsequently heated, can withstand an exceedingly high degree of fire. (5)
Thus ends the seventh [stage], the processing by steaming (*svedana*) for that which has had its flavor extracted (*utthāpitarasa*).
[In another text, the steaming is as follows:
With black mustard, salt, fire-root (*vahnimūlaka*), coriander, and *kalāśaka*—[these are used for the steaming].
This sudation of mercury over a mild fire is performed with water from chaff husks.

When that which is to be sweated is suspended inside a cloth pouch within a vessel of sour gruel and medicinal leaves, and heated over a stove fire while being rocked back and forth, this is the *dolayantra* (swinging apparatus).
Having folded the cloth into four layers and enclosed it within a crucible,
the mercury should be heated over a mild fire so that it does not suffer depletion.
The wise person should cause the mercury to undergo sudation for one day with *vyoṣa*, fresh *śigru* root, *mayūra-mūlaka*, and *āsuri*, along with *kāñjika*.

Silver, sesame, honey, gold, and lead are killed by means of lead (*nāga*).
Just as the procedure for copper has been declared, that same procedure applies to the killing of these five.

[Commentary: By means of realgar (*manaḥśilā*), lead is killed; by yellow orpiment (*haritāla*), tin (*vaṅga*); by cinnabar (*hiṅgula*), iron; by pure sulphur (*śuddhagandhaka*), copper; by sesame and honey, silver; and by lead, gold is killed.
Then, according to the prescribed method:
having prepared either a leaf or a powder of copper, the wise one should release it separately;
and he should take pure sulphur powder, doubled in amount compared to the copper.
Having ground that [substance] with the juice of *kumārī*, or with milk if that is unavailable,
one should insert a copper leaf into the interior of two cakes made from it.
Having placed that inside a pair of earthenware bowls and sealed them with clay,
and having smeared the seam with cloth and clay, one should place that packet into a cauldron.
Having placed small pieces of copper in a cauldron, one should then ignite a fire.
When it has cooled after burning, the wise should take up the copper as it becomes "dead" (melted/solidified).
Alternatively, having made a leaf or a powder of copper, one should then add double the amount of pure copper and powdered sulphur in the juice of *kumārī*.
Alternatively, having thoroughly kneaded *nāga* with milk and made two cakes, one should place the previously prepared powder of copper leaf in the middle;

then, having placed the two cakes in a pair of earthen bowls (*śarāva*), smeared the seam with cloth-clay (*vastramṛttikā*), and coated them all over with clay, one should place the pair of bowls inside a cauldron, fill the cauldron with chaff, and extinguish the fire. 1.
Then, having been heated until it becomes cool, the copper is to be taken as killed.
Thus ends the procedure for killing copper.
By the same procedure by which the copper was killed here with sulphur, the five metals beginning with lead (nāga) are to be killed when required.
Thus ends the procedure for the killing of the six metals.
[5] Now, regarding the preparation of the three-fold dietary diamond and the five-fold killing: one should remove the stalk of a citron (*bījapūra*) and create a hollow cavity.
Having placed a genuine diamond in the center of that, one should cover it with a stalk.
One should wrap a whole citron with cloth and clay;
then, one should prepare a pit measuring one cubit in length, depth, and width.
Once that pit has been filled with the powder prepared by Cāṇakya, one should cover its opening with a bowl made of *bījapūraka* fruit;
thereafter, one should cast fire into its center.
Once it has burned and become cool, this ritual procedure should be performed again and again with ever-new *bījapūraka* fruits for nine times.
Having transformed it into a very subtle female donkey in the night, one should cast that ball [of essence] inside;
the ball is placed within a pair of earthenware bowls (*śarāva*).
A pit previously prepared and established by the followers of Cāṇakya should be filled again;
its surface smeared with cloth and clay, the wise practitioner should cook [the substance] within the pit.
One should repeatedly cook it nine times with these mares;
then, there shall be a branch of the royal jujube tree consisting of tender sprouts.
Then, having taken that [substance], the wise one should make an opening in its interior;
having placed *nesa* and asafoetida (*hiṅgu*) below and above, he should insert that diamond.
Then, with clay from a garment, one should fill the branches and sprouts so they are without gaps;
this is done in nine ways according to the previous method in the pit previously dug.
Having made a hole in a pill composed of asafoetida, one should place a diamond inside it;
then, having covered the opening with asafoetida, there should be a base of *muṣarī* and *māṣa*.
Having cast it into a vessel filled with that oil, one should ignite a fire beneath it;
in this manner, using the proper technique, the process should be performed nine times for each fresh pellet of asafoetida.
By means of the ritual procedure, a genuine diamond (*hīraka*) clearly comes into being.
Having ground it with *thūthā* and *viḍa*, the wise one causes it to be digested in the liquid.
[Having uprooted the stalk of a citron (*bījapūra*), having hollowed out the middle and made a cavity therein, one should place the genuine diamond inside and [cover it] on top...]

Having covered it with its stalk and wrapped the entire *bījapūraka* fruit in clay, one should then dig a pit one cubit deep, one cubit wide, and one cubit long; having filled it with dried cow-dung cakes (*chāṇaka*) and placed the *bījapūraka* therein, one should cover the opening with a potsherd and apply fire to the cow-dung cakes.

Then, once it has burned and cooled down, one should first feel shame; thereafter, bringing a second citron (*bījapūra*) as before and performing everything as previously described, one should place the diamond and the citron into the pit, ignite the chaff, and when it has cooled, the diamond is to be taken from the center of the citron.
In this manner, that very same diamond should be cooked nine times with nine successive citrons.
Then, having prepared a clay mold using the ash of a mare’s dung, one should place that very diamond in the center of it.

Next, having placed that mold inside a pair of earthen bowls (*śarāva*) and smeared them all over with cloth and clay, one should fill a previously dug pit with cow-dung cakes; then, having placed the pair of bowls in the middle of that pit, fire should be ignited.
Then, once it has cooled, one should again place that same diamond in the midst of a ball of other *vaḍavāikā* plants, ignite it in the same manner, and extract the diamond.

In this way, it should be cooked nine times with nine different *vaḍavāikā* plants. Having brought a tender branch in the form of a sprout of *rājabadarī*, one should make a hole in it, place *nesahiṅgu* both below and above it, and [place the diamond] in the middle of the hole.
Having thrown that very diamond into it and covered it with cloth and earth, one should first cook it in a pit filled with dried cow-dung.
Then, having again placed the diamond inside the hollow of a fresh sprout of a jujube branch, it should be cooked in the same manner in the pit.
In this way, nine times over, that same diamond should be cooked with ever-fresh sprouts of royal jujube branches.

Then, having made a hole in the middle of a large lump of asafoetida (*hiṅgu*), one should place that very diamond inside, cover the opening with asafoetida, and place a layer of black gram (*māṣa*) on top; thereafter, having placed that asafoetida-lump into a vessel filled with oil, a fire should be kindled beneath it. 4.

Then again, in the same manner, [it should be done] nine times with fresh pieces of asafoetida (*hiṅgu*). Thus, that very diamond (*hīraka*) should be cooked nine times with ever-fresh pieces of asafoetida.
Having ground that diamond with *thūthā* and *viḍa* salt, the diamond should be slowly digested (*jāraṇīya*) in the previously mentioned liquid.
Thus ends the first [section] on the digestion (*jāraṇa*) of diamonds using food and medicinal substances.

with these, a wise person should wrap high-quality diamonds to ensure their perfection. Rsdhy_289[188]
Having placed that [substance] among the roots of the *sūraṇa* and other small tubers, and having wrapped it with cloth and clay,
one should apply the *puṭa* on the ground in a shape resembling a cock.
And the packets should be given repeatedly with impurities from the ears, small tubers of the suraṇa plant,
and fresh earth from clothing.
And by means of twenty-one applications using cock-poultices on the ground,
wise men easily bring forth diamonds from the path of food (*annapatha*).
Having taken the ear-wax of female buffaloes and wrapped high-quality diamonds with that wax, one then [uses] those diamonds encased in that wax.

Having made holes in the small bulbs of the *sūraṇa* plant and having placed [the diamond] therein, one should smear it all over with cloth-dirt (*karpaṭamṛttikā*) and place it on the ground in a "cock-pit" (*kurkuṭapuṭa*).

Then, taking the diamond again and wrapping it likewise with buffalo-ear-wax (*mahiṣīkarṇamala*), one should place it in the middle of a small *sūraṇa* bulb, smear it all over with cloth-dirt, and [bury it] on the ground with dried cow-dung (*chāṇaka*).
A chicken-shaped pouch should be provided.

In this manner, having wrapped it repeatedly twenty-one times with buffalo-ear wax, having placed small turnips (*sūraṇa*) within them, and having set the chicken-pouches upon the ground, the "diamonds for the path of food" (*annapathyahīrakāḥ*) are to be prepared.
Thus ends the second procedure: the preparation of diamonds for the path of food.
One should roll out the soft leaves of the *bhūmyāmardakī* plant;
having placed diamonds within a ball made from that [dough], one should fashion a *golakam* (ball).
Having placed it in a hollowed-out leaf-cup and wrapped it with clay from a wall-crack,
one should apply a seal (puṭa) upon the ground resembling a cock.

Fresh, fresh portions should be offered repeatedly; all sixty-four types of *kurkuṭa* cakes should be given, and diamonds should be made into a path for the food. Having rolled out the tender leaves of the *mardakī* (earth-crusher) plant—that is, the *bhūmiphoḍī*—and having formed them into balls...

Having placed high-quality diamonds in the center, formed them into balls, and placed them inside a pair of earthen saucers, one should apply a cloth-and-clay mixture at the seam and place it on the ground in a "cock-pit" (kurkuṭapuṭa) fashion.

Then, again in the same manner, having placed diamonds within a mass of *bhūmyāmardakī* on the ground, formed them into balls, placed them in a pair of earthen saucers, and applied a cloth-and-clay mixture at the seam, [one should place it] on the ground...
A "cock-pit" (kurkuṭapuṭa) should be given. 2.
In this manner, with sixty-four new "cock-pits" of balls made from masses of Bhūmyāmardakī leaves, those diamonds should be placed on the ground, and their paths [of movement] should be prepared. 3.
This is the meaning. 4.
They become cooked as if with food and are digested along with the juices.
Thus ends the third procedure regarding the preparation of the path for diamonds.

Having brought a baked skull-cup, many pits should be made [within it].

One should throw high-quality iron into them; then, having repeatedly blown upon it until it becomes the color of a flame, those who know the procedure should fashion a crucible from it using the remains of the deceased.
Human urine, *thauhara* milk, and [the other substance] mixed together in equal parts—
one should repeatedly heat a crucible with these two until it is molten.
Then, having made cavities in new earthen vessels and placed diamonds within them, one should blow upon those very [diamonds];
once they have been blown upon, one should sprinkle them with the mixture.
Having blown [the bellows] seven times according to this method, one should repeatedly extinguish it;
such [results] as those occur in the first blowing, while in the second, they become like *jāmbūnada* gold.
